does: Collapses tender leaves with brief heat, so that they turn soft and dark and lose most of their bulk.

intro.what: Wilting briefly heats tender leaves until they collapse and lose bulk.
intro.why: It teaches you to stop at a texture change instead of leaving delicate greens to release more water.

how: Wash the leaves and leave the water that clings to them.
Melt a little fat in a wide pan over medium heat.
Add the leaves by the handful, turning them as they fall.
Take them off the heat as soon as the last leaf has collapsed, and press out the water.

cues.text: Dark green, glossy and limp, a fraction of the raw heap.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the leaves on the heat, so that they go on shedding water and turn slimy.
mistakes.fix: Stop the moment they collapse, and drain them.

quiz.question: What change is sought when wilting tender leaves?
choices: They form a crisp dry crust.
They soften and collapse from their raw bulk.
quiz.because: Brief heat softens the leaves so a large raw heap becomes a smaller limp mass.

quiz.question: How should leaves be added to the pan?
choices: By handfuls, turning them as they collapse.
Pressed into a dense unmoving stack.
Dry them completely and add the whole pile without turning.
quiz.because: Gradual additions and turning expose fresh leaves as the earlier ones lose volume.

quiz.question: Which appearance fits wilted greens?
choices: Pale rigid leaves holding the original heap.
Dark green glossy limp leaves with much less bulk.
Blackened crisp fragments around dry stems.
quiz.because: Collapse and gloss distinguish wilting from leaving leaves raw or frying them until crisp.

quiz.question: The leaves became slimy while continuing to shed water. What would you change next time?
choices: Leave them heating until all structure disappears.
Cover and keep cooking after collapse.
Remove them when they collapse and drain them.
quiz.because: Continued heating beyond collapse can over-soften tender leaves and release excess liquid.
